newsitem.title: USA: Treasury's Hawke says charter issue a top priority.
newsitem.headline: Treasury's Hawke says charter issue a top priority.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury Department has given a high priority to completing the reform of the thrift industry's insurance system, Savings Association Insurance Fund (SAIF), John Hawke, undersecretary for domestic finance, said on Thursday.
"One of our top priorities is following through and realizing the final implications of the BIF/SAIF legislation," Hawke said in a speech at the Brookings Institute, a Washington think-tank.
To merge the banking-industry fund with the thrift fund, separate charters for thrifts must be eliminated, Hawke noted.
"That essentially forces our attention to the rationalization of differences in the charters that banks and thrifts operate under," Hawke said.

Discussing the upcoming overhaul of Depression-era laws barring banks from engaging in non-banking activities, Hawke said bank subsidiaries could expand into new areas without putting the financial solvency of their parents at risk.

"We believe that it is possible to achieve protections for the bank that are equally effective as those that would protect the bank in the case of activities that are conducted through affiliates," Hawke said.
In part, that could be achieved by forbidding banks from including as regulatory capital any investment in a subsidiary that engages in non-banking activity, Hawke said.

"The banks should be required to meet its regulatory capital requirements on a stand-alone basis without regard to its investment in its subsidiary," Hawke said. "You should subtract out the amount of the investment in the subsidiary as an asset on the bank's balance sheet with an equivilent charge to capital."
"Extensions of credit by the bank to its subsidiary would have to be collateralized," he added.
Legislative reform of the financial system may be passed in chunks but should be consistent, Hawke said.
"Temporary moratoriums and stop-gap legislation aimed at specific court decisions and regulatory rulings should be avoided," Hawke said.
